Getting started with opengwasr

Source: vignettes/opengwasr.Rmd
opengwasr.Rmd

opengwasr gives you OpenGWAS data in R: Analysis metadata, top hits, Associations and LD. Every query function takes a Source as its first argument, which says where the query is answered. This vignette uses the API Source, og_api(), which queries the OpenGWAS API over the network. A later release adds a Local Source for Store Releases downloaded to your own machine. Code written against og_api() will work with it unchanged.

You never handle the API’s Jobs, polling, paging or variant encodings yourself. Each call waits for its answer and returns a plain data.frame. When a query can’t be answered exactly as you asked, opengwasr stops with an error that says why. It never quietly gives you a different answer.

Status. Every chunk runs, replayed from responses recorded against the development Data API on 23 November 2026, except the ones marked illustrative, each with its reason: the planned og_rho() (it needs a Data API endpoint that doesn’t exist yet), the error you get with no key, and the error for an ambiguous identifier (no identifier is ambiguous in today’s catalogue).

Developer note: The API responses in this vignette were recorded against the development Data API, directly, with a developer key (see vignettes/recordings.R). Once the OpenGWAS Gateway is live (#18), re-record through it, so the vignettes show the access users will have.

The examples follow one Mendelian randomization question: does body mass index (BMI) affect coronary artery disease (CAD)?

library(opengwasr)

Credentials

Your OpenGWAS token

opengwasr signs in to the OpenGWAS Gateway with the same token ieugwasr uses. Get it from your OpenGWAS profile and add it to your .Renviron file, which you can open with usethis::edit_r_environ():

OPENGWAS_JWT=<your token>

Restart R so the new setting is read. opengwasr never prints your token, and never writes it into errors or logs.

Not yet available. The Gateway doesn’t serve the new OpenGWAS API yet. Until it does, only the developer access below works.

Developer access (development and tests only)

Before the Gateway is live, opengwasr’s developers reach the Data API directly with a developer key. This is for developing opengwasr, running its live tests and recording these vignettes. Don’t use it for analyses.

OPENGWAS_URL=http://localhost:6433
OPENGWAS_DEV_KEY=<developer key>
OPENGWAS_DEV_USER=opengwasr-dev

When OPENGWAS_DEV_KEY is set, og_api() sends it to OPENGWAS_URL, naming OPENGWAS_DEV_USER (default opengwasr-dev) as the user. Keep these settings in a .Renviron that is never committed.

Creating the API Source 

src <- og_api()
src
## <og_api_source>
## • URL: http://localhost:6433
## • Signed in with: OPENGWAS_DEV_KEY (as opengwasr-dev)
## • Timeout: 3600 s
## • Jobs in flight: at most 4

og_api() takes url, timeout (seconds to wait for any one call before giving up) and max_in_flight (how many Jobs one call may run at once). Each defaults to an option (opengwasr.url, opengwasr.timeout, opengwasr.max_in_flight), so you can set it once for a session. A fourth option, opengwasr.progress, turns the progress display off when FALSE; it is on in interactive sessions by default.

options(opengwasr.timeout = 600)
src <- og_api()

Without a key, og_api() stops straight away:

This is illustrative, not recorded: the vignettes always run with a key set.

# illustrative
Error in `og_api()`:
! No OpenGWAS key found.
ℹ Set `OPENGWAS_DEV_KEY` in your .Renviron to your developer key, then restart R.

That error has class opengwasr_auth. A key the API doesn’t accept is reported on the first query that needs one, such as og_user() (og_status() doesn’t, because the API serves it without a key), with the API’s own message, Invalid bearer token, and class opengwasr_unauthorized. Printing the Source shows the setting that supplied the key, never the key.

Checking your access

og_status() reports whether the API is up. The API serves /api/status without a key, so og_status() works even with a wrong one (building the Source with og_api() still needs a key to be set). og_user() reports who you are signed in as, and your allowance, and is the call that checks your key.

og_status(src)
## ── OpenGWAS API ──
## ✔ Ready
## • Most Associations one Job returns: 100,000
## • Unread Job results kept for: 1 h
## • Jobs one user may have queued: 100
og_user(src)
## ── Signed in ──
## • User: opengwasr-dev
## • Tier: gateway
## • Allowance: 1,000
## • Jobs running at once: 10

Both return a list, so scripts can read the fields. You can have up to 10 Jobs running and up to 100 queued at any time; opengwasr keeps within both.

Finding Analyses

An Analysis is one statistical analysis of one trait. Each lives in a GWAS Store, a published collection of harmonised GWAS summary statistics with an OGS-* id, and is named <store_id>:<analysis_id>, such as OGS-00011:GCST90029007.

By identifier 

info <- og_analyses(src, c("OGS-00011:GCST90029007", "OGS-00011:GCST003116"))
info[, c("id", "analysis_label", "assigned_ancestry", "sample_size",
         "outcome_type", "stored_effect_scale")]
##                       id          analysis_label assigned_ancestry sample_size
## 1 OGS-00011:GCST90029007         Body mass index               EUR      532396
## 2   OGS-00011:GCST003116 Coronary artery disease               EUR      187599
##   outcome_type stored_effect_scale
## 1   continuous                  sd
## 2       binary              log_or

Analyses come back in the order you gave them, one per identifier. The metadata includes the trait (analysis_label, trait_ontology_id), the Assigned Ancestry, sample sizes (sample_size, sample_size_kind, n_cases, n_controls), how effects are scaled (stored_effect_scale, original_sd, original_sd_method), the publication and the licence.

Legacy OpenGWAS identifiers

Identifiers from Legacy OpenGWAS, the OpenGWAS service ieugwasr calls, are accepted where they name exactly one Analysis. The requested_id column shows what you asked for:

og_analyses(src, c("ukb-b-19953", "ebi-a-GCST003116"))[, c("requested_id", "id", "analysis_label")]
##       requested_id                    id          analysis_label
## 1      ukb-b-19953 OGS-00009:ukb-b-19953   Body mass index (BMI)
## 2 ebi-a-GCST003116  OGS-00011:GCST003116 Coronary artery disease

An identifier that names no Analysis is an error, of class opengwasr_analysis_not_found. For most identifiers the API says only that it found nothing, so the message just names the identifier; where the API gives a reason, as it does for a Legacy OpenGWAS family it doesn’t hold, the message quotes it and e$api_reasons keeps it. Some Legacy OpenGWAS identifier families aren’t held by any GWAS Store:

og_analyses(src, "ieu-a-2")
## Error in `og_analyses()`:
## ! Identifiers that name no Analysis:
## ✖ ieu-a-2: OpenGWAS batch ieu-a is not held by any Store

Some legacy identifiers now point to a later release of the same analysis. For example, finn-b-I9_CHD points to FinnGen release 13, OGS-00017:finngen-r13-I9_CHD. opengwasr answers with the successor, and warns you, because its numbers differ from the ones Legacy OpenGWAS served:

og_analyses(src, "finn-b-I9_CHD")[, c("requested_id", "id", "analysis_label")]
## Warning in og_analyses(src, "finn-b-I9_CHD"): `finn-b-I9_CHD` now points to a later release of that analysis, "OGS-00017:finngen-r13-I9_CHD", whose numbers differ from the ones Legacy OpenGWAS served.
## ℹ Ask for "OGS-00017:finngen-r13-I9_CHD" by name to silence this warning.
##    requested_id                           id                     analysis_label
## 1 finn-b-I9_CHD OGS-00017:finngen-r13-I9_CHD Major coronary heart disease event

The warning has class opengwasr_legacy_successor, and carries the identifier you gave in w$requested_id and the successor in w$id. Catch it with tryCatch() to stop instead, or muffle it with withCallingHandlers(). Every query function that takes Analyses does the same.

If an identifier could name more than one Analysis, opengwasr stops and lists them, with class opengwasr_ambiguous_analysis. No identifier is ambiguous in today’s catalogue. This is what the error would look like, for a hypothetical bare GCST90000001 held by two GWAS Stores (illustrative, not recorded, because there is nothing to provoke it with):

# illustrative
Error in `og_analyses()`:
! `GCST90000001` names more than one Analysis.
ℹ Use one of: "OGS-00011:GCST90000001", "OGS-00012:GCST90000001".

Pinning a Store Release

Each GWAS Store is published as a series of immutable Store Releases. Without releases, opengwasr uses the one Store Release the API serves for each GWAS Store, and sends that choice to the API rather than leaving it to the API’s default of every configured Store Release. You can pin Store Releases with releases, which every query function accepts. Give a GWAS Store id, such as "OGS-00011", to use the one Store Release it serves (if any GWAS Store ever serves several, the API doesn’t say which is latest, so opengwasr stops with opengwasr_release_selection_required and lists them, whether you named that GWAS Store or left releases out), or "<store_id>/<release_id>" to pin a particular one:

og_analyses(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90029007",
            releases = "OGS-00011/OGS-00011-completed")[, c("id", "release_id")]
##                       id          release_id
## 1 OGS-00011:GCST90029007 OGS-00011-completed

To reproduce an analysis later, record the store_id and release_id columns that come back with every Association (see Provenance).

Browsing the catalogue

Without identifiers, og_analyses() reads the whole catalogue, page by page, with a progress bar. The whole catalogue is tens of thousands of Analyses, so this example reads one GWAS Store, the UK Biobank analyses of OGS-00009, by pinning it with releases. Leave releases out for everything:

catalogue <- og_analyses(src, releases = "OGS-00009")
nrow(catalogue)
## [1] 2514
bmi <- subset(catalogue, grepl("body mass index", analysis_label, ignore.case = TRUE) &
                assigned_ancestry %in% "EUR" & outcome_type == "continuous")
head(bmi[, c("id", "analysis_label", "sample_size")], 3)
##                         id        analysis_label sample_size
## 1345 OGS-00009:ukb-b-19953 Body mass index (BMI)      461460
## 1479  OGS-00009:ukb-b-2303 Body mass index (BMI)      454884

Variants are named by ALID

opengwasr names every variant by its ALID, as the GWAS Stores and LD Stores do. An ALID is chromosome:position:A1:A2, such as 16:53767042:C:T:

  • chromosome is 1 to 22, X, Y or MT, with no chr prefix. Other contig names (such as GRCh38 alt contigs) are kept as given, as the GWAS Stores keep them.
  • position is on GRCh38, one-based, as in a VCF file. An indel is left-aligned, and its position is that of the first base of its alleles.
  • A1 and A2 are the two alleles, upper case. When they are the same length (an SNV, or a substitution of several bases), they are in alphabetical order: C:T, never T:C. When their lengths differ (an indel), the GRCh38 reference allele comes first: the insertion 5:75701728:A:AAAAT, the deletion 1:827587:GGGGCC:G. An insertion and a deletion of the same sequence at one position are therefore two different variants.
  • A1 is the effect allele. Every Association’s effect_allele is the A1 of its alid, so beta, z and eaf always refer to A1, and the sign of an LD r refers to it too.
  • An ALID names exactly two alleles. A site with more alleles appears as several ALIDs at the same position, one per pair of alleles a GWAS Store holds, and one rsID can name several of them.

ALIDs are the same in every GWAS Store and LD Store on GRCh38, so the same variant joins across Analyses, Store Releases and LD. Use og_variants_rsid() and og_variants_chrpos() (below) to find the ALIDs for rsIDs or positions.

ALIDs for your own data

To join your own summary statistics to OpenGWAS data, give them ALIDs with og_alid(). It takes a data frame with a chromosome, a GRCh38 position and two alleles, and returns it with an alid column added and the alleles oriented to match. Here my_gwas is a small made-up data frame standing in for your own data:

my_gwas <- data.frame(
  chromosome    = c("16", "chr18", "5", "1"),
  position      = c(53767042, 60161902, 75701728, 827587),
  effect_allele = c("T", "c", "AAAAT", "G"),
  other_allele  = c("C", "T", "A", "GGGGCC"),
  eaf           = c(0.58, 0.24, 0.13, 0.04),
  beta          = c(-0.076, 0.055, -0.025, 0.12)
)
og_alid(my_gwas)
## ℹ Swapped the alleles of 1 variant to match its ALID: `beta` negated, `eaf`
##   replaced by 1 - `eaf`.
## ! 2 indels have no ALID, because no allele is declared the reference. Name it
##   with `reference`.
##   chromosome position effect_allele other_allele  eaf   beta            alid
## 1         16 53767042             C            T 0.42  0.076 16:53767042:C:T
## 2         18 60161902             C            T 0.24  0.055 18:60161902:C:T
## 3          5 75701728         AAAAT            A 0.13 -0.025            <NA>
## 4          1   827587             G       GGGGCC 0.04  0.120            <NA>
  • SNVs and substitutions are always oriented. Their alleles are sorted, so A1 comes first. The first variant’s effect allele T isn’t A1, so its alleles are swapped, beta is negated (and z, if there is one), and eaf becomes 1 − eaf. The second variant’s chr18 and c are normalised to 18 and C.
  • Indels need their reference allele declared. An indel’s ALID puts the GRCh38 reference allele first, and the alleles alone can’t say which one that is: at a repeat, an insertion and a deletion can have the same two alleles. Without reference, an indel’s alid is NA, and a message gives the count. This is the same rule the GWAS Stores were built by, so an ALID og_alid() makes always matches theirs.

If your data came from a VCF, or otherwise says which allele is the reference, pass reference: "other_allele" or "effect_allele" when one of those columns is always the reference, or the name of a column holding the reference allele:

og_alid(my_gwas, reference = "other_allele")
## ℹ Swapped the alleles of 3 variants to match their ALIDs: `beta` negated, `eaf`
##   replaced by 1 - `eaf`.
##   chromosome position effect_allele other_allele  eaf   beta               alid
## 1         16 53767042             C            T 0.42  0.076    16:53767042:C:T
## 2         18 60161902             C            T 0.24  0.055    18:60161902:C:T
## 3          5 75701728             A        AAAAT 0.87  0.025 5:75701728:A:AAAAT
## 4          1   827587        GGGGCC            G 0.96 -0.120  1:827587:GGGGCC:G

reference is used only for indels. og_alid() assumes two things it can’t check without the reference genome: alleles are on the forward strand, and indels are already left-aligned, as in a normalised VCF. The column names are arguments (chromosome, position, effect_allele, other_allele, eaf, beta, z), with the defaults shown. eaf, beta and z are adjusted when the data has them.

Top hits

og_tophits() returns each Analysis’s Associations at or below a p-value threshold (default 5e-8), strongest first. It clumps them by default, keeping one variant per independent signal; the LD operations vignette explains how. Here, clump = FALSE shows every top hit:

top <- og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST003116", clump = FALSE, limit = 5)
## Warning in og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST003116", clump = FALSE, limit = 5): OGS-00011:GCST003116 has more than 5 top hits at p <= 5e-08; only the strongest 5 were returned.
## ℹ Raise `limit` (at most 10,000) for more.
head(top[, c("rsid", "alid", "beta", "se", "pval", "association_status")], 4)
##         rsid           alid       beta          se         pval
## 1  rs2891168 9:22098620:A:G -0.1933591 0.009185791 2.296241e-98
## 2  rs4977574 9:22098575:A:G -0.1929106 0.009185791 6.425124e-98
## 3 rs10738610 9:22123767:A:C -0.1936836 0.009292603 1.772656e-96
## 4 rs10757275 9:22106226:A:G  0.1930436 0.009269714 2.558808e-96
##   association_status
## 1           observed
## 2           observed
## 3           observed
## 4           observed
  • limit (default 1,000, here 5) caps the top hits returned per Analysis. When it cuts any off, you get the warning above.
  • threshold must be one the GWAS Store indexes. Each GWAS Store indexes 5e-8, 5e-6 and 5e-4, and the API refuses anything looser:
og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST003116", threshold = 1e-3, clump = FALSE, limit = 5)
## Error in `og_tophits()`:
## ! threshold must be at most 0.0005, the loosest p-value the Top-Hit Index of OGS-00011 holds

That error has class opengwasr_unsupported_threshold, a kind of opengwasr_refusal, and carries the thresholds the GWAS Store indexes, as the API listed them, in e$indexed_thresholds.

Associations

og_associations() returns the Associations for a set of variants in a set of Analyses: for example, the outcome data for your instruments. Variants can be rsIDs or ALIDs, mixed.

assoc <- og_associations(
  src,
  variants = c("rs1421085", "16:53767042:C:T", "rs6567160", "rs34159589", "rs999999999"),
  analyses = c("OGS-00011:GCST90029007", "OGS-00011:GCST003116")
)
## Warning in og_associations(src, variants = c("rs1421085", "16:53767042:C:T", :
## 1 rsID is in none of these Analyses' GWAS Stores, so it has no Associations:
## rs999999999.
assoc[, c("id", "rsid", "alid", "beta", "se", "pval", "association_status")]
##                       id       rsid               alid         beta          se
## 1 OGS-00011:GCST90029007 rs34159589 5:75701728:A:AAAAT -0.025441924 0.002000809
## 2 OGS-00011:GCST90029007  rs1421085    16:53767042:C:T  0.075834384 0.001968384
## 3 OGS-00011:GCST90029007  rs6567160    18:60161902:C:T  0.054658253 0.002292633
## 4   OGS-00011:GCST003116 rs34159589 5:75701728:A:AAAAT -0.003017932 0.009841919
## 5   OGS-00011:GCST003116  rs1421085    16:53767042:C:T  0.029665306 0.009628296
## 6   OGS-00011:GCST003116  rs6567160    18:60161902:C:T  0.057734668 0.010559082
##            pval association_status
## 1  4.830139e-37            imputed
## 2  0.000000e+00           observed
## 3 1.260915e-125           observed
## 4  7.591169e-01            imputed
## 5  2.062688e-03           observed
## 6  4.557239e-08           observed
  • An rsID can name several ALIDs, and opengwasr asks for every one of them. It never picks one for you. rs1421085 names 16:53767042:A:G and 16:53767042:C:T; these Analyses hold only the second, which you also asked for by its ALID, so it appears once per Analysis. rs34159589 names 5:75701728:A:AAAAT and 5:75701728:AAAAT:AAAATAAAT; again only the first has Associations here.
  • Every match is returned: if an Analysis held Associations for both ALIDs of an rsID, you would get both.
  • Every Association has an alid, so you can always join by it. It has an rsid too, except where a GWAS Store holds the variant with no rsID: rsid is then NA.
  • An rsID that no GWAS Store holds is reported in a warning (class opengwasr_unresolved_variants, with the rsIDs in its ids field), never dropped quietly.
  • Imputed Associations are included (association_status == "imputed"). Pass observed_only = TRUE to leave them out. See Imputed Associations.

There is no LD-proxy option. Reference-Completed Store Releases already hold an Imputed Association for most variants a source didn’t report.

PheWAS, regions and variant lookups

og_phewas() returns the Associations of one or more variants (rsIDs and ALIDs) across Analyses, at p ≤ threshold (default 1e-8). By default it searches every Analysis of every GWAS Store; releases narrows the search, and analyses names the Analyses to look in. An rsID is resolved to every ALID it names, and opengwasr runs one PheWAS per ALID and combines them in the order you gave the variants. Here, the Associations of rs1421085 at p ≤ 1e-50 in one GWAS Store:

ph <- og_phewas(src, "rs1421085", threshold = 1e-50, releases = "OGS-00011")
nrow(ph)
## [1] 27
head(ph[, c("id", "analysis_label", "beta", "pval")], 4)
##                       id                              analysis_label
## 1   OGS-00011:GCST002047 Educational attainment (college completion)
## 2   OGS-00011:GCST004461             Low-grade serous ovarian cancer
## 3 OGS-00011:GCST90025994                             Body mass index
## 4 OGS-00011:GCST90029007                             Body mass index
##          beta          pval
## 1 -0.41119424  0.000000e+00
## 2 -3.22208393  0.000000e+00
## 3  0.08162382 2.766768e-322
## 4  0.07583438  0.000000e+00

pval is 0 where it underflows; z stays exact. limit (default 1,000, at most 10,000) applies to each ALID, not to all the variants together. When it cuts a PheWAS off you get a warning, as for top hits.

og_range() returns every Association in a stretch of one chromosome. Positions are on GRCh38, one-based and inclusive. A range over 10 Mb, or over more than 10 Analyses, is split into several Jobs for you:

locus <- og_range(src, "OGS-00011:GCST003116", chromosome = "9",
                  start = 22090000, end = 22130000)
table(locus$association_status)
## 
##  imputed observed 
##       19       85

og_variants_rsid() and og_variants_chrpos() translate rsIDs and GRCh38 positions into ALIDs, using the GWAS Stores’ own variant tables. You get each ALID once for every GWAS Store that holds it:

og_variants_rsid(src, "rs34159589", releases = "OGS-00011")
##                         alid chromosome effect_allele other_allele position
## 1         5:75701728:A:AAAAT          5             A        AAAAT 75701728
## 2 5:75701728:AAAAT:AAAATAAAT          5         AAAAT    AAAATAAAT 75701728
##            release_id       rsid  store_id
## 1 OGS-00011-completed rs34159589 OGS-00011
## 2 OGS-00011-completed rs34159589 OGS-00011
og_variants_chrpos(src, "16:53767042", releases = "OGS-00011")
##              alid chromosome effect_allele other_allele position
## 1 16:53767042:A:G         16             A            G 53767042
## 2 16:53767042:C:T         16             C            T 53767042
##            release_id      rsid  store_id
## 1 OGS-00011-completed rs1421085 OGS-00011
## 2 OGS-00011-completed rs1421085 OGS-00011

Every match is returned: one position can hold several ALIDs, and one rsID can name several.

Correlation between Analyses: the Rho Matrix

Planned. og_rho() needs a Data API endpoint that doesn’t exist yet.

Analyses in one GWAS Store often share participants, and their traits can be correlated, so their z-scores are correlated even at variants with no effect on either trait. Rho is that correlation under the null: the traits’ phenotypic correlation times the Analyses’ proportion of sample overlap. A GWAS Store with a Dense Layout can carry a Rho Matrix: Rho for every pair of its Analyses, estimated by opengwasdb from their Observed null z-scores. Methods that combine Analyses and must allow for sample overlap, such as multivariable MR or multi-trait analyses, can use it rather than estimate it again.

og_rho() will return the whole matrix for a GWAS Store, or the part for the Analyses you choose:

rho_all <- og_rho(src, store = "OGS-00009")
rho <- og_rho(src, analyses = c("OGS-00009:ukb-b-19953", "OGS-00009:ukb-b-2303", "OGS-00009:ukb-b-11842"))
  • It returns a symmetric matrix named by Analysis id, with 1 on the diagonal. A pair with too few shared null variants to estimate Rho is NA.
  • og_provenance(rho)$n_null is the matching matrix of how many null variants supported each pair, and og_provenance(rho) also gives the settings that produced it, such as the null z threshold.
  • Give store for the whole matrix, or analyses for part of it. Rho is estimated within one GWAS Store, so all the analyses must share one.
  • A GWAS Store without a Rho Matrix is refused, with class opengwasr_rho_unavailable, a kind of opengwasr_refusal.

What the columns mean

Every function that returns Associations (og_tophits(), og_associations(), og_phewas(), og_range()) returns the same columns:

Column Meaning
id The Analysis, as <store_id>:<analysis_id>
store_id, analysis_id, analysis_label Its GWAS Store, its identifier within the GWAS Store, and its trait
alid, rsid, chromosome, position The variant, on GRCh38 (see ALIDs). rsid is NA for a variant with no rsID
effect_allele, other_allele, eaf Its alleles (A1 and A2 of the ALID), and the effect allele’s frequency
beta, se The effect of one copy of the effect allele, and its standard error
z, pval The z-score and the p-value
effect_scale The scale beta and se are on: "sd", "log_or", or "original" when you ask for original_units = TRUE
n, sample_size_kind, ncase, ncontrol Sample size, and what kind of count it is
association_status "observed" or "imputed"
release_id The Store Release the Association came from

Effects and p-values

z and se are the GWAS Store’s own. opengwasr adds beta = z * se, and computes pval from the p-value the API sends, so it matches the API exactly. All of them are computed the same way everywhere.

top <- og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90029007", clump = FALSE, limit = 3)
## Warning in og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90029007", clump = FALSE, limit = 3): OGS-00011:GCST90029007 has more than 3 top hits at p <= 5e-08; only the strongest 3 were returned.
## ℹ Raise `limit` (at most 10,000) for more.
top[, c("rsid", "z", "se", "beta", "pval")]
##         rsid         z          se        beta pval
## 1 rs56094641 -38.53421 0.001968384 -0.07585011    0
## 2 rs11642015 -38.53265 0.001968384 -0.07584705    0
## 3 rs62048402  38.52727 0.001968384  0.07583645    0

When |z| is above about 38.5, the p-value is smaller than R can represent (about 1e-323), so pval underflows to 0. z stays exact, so rank or filter the strongest signals by abs(z), not by pval.

Effect scale and original units

The effect_scale column says what beta and se mean:

  • "sd": per standard deviation of the trait. Continuous traits are stored this way, so effects are comparable across Analyses.
  • "log_or": log odds, for binary traits.

Some binary Analyses are stored per SD rather than as log odds. effect_scale says which, so check it rather than assuming from the trait.

For a continuous trait in its original units, pass original_units = TRUE. opengwasr multiplies beta and se by the Analysis’s recorded phenotype SD (original_sd in og_analyses()), and effect_scale becomes "original":

per_sd <- og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90624700", clump = FALSE, limit = 5)
original <- og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90624700", clump = FALSE, limit = 5,
                       original_units = TRUE)
head(per_sd[, c("rsid", "beta", "se", "effect_scale")], 3)
##         rsid        beta         se effect_scale
## 1  rs1421085  0.09583174 0.00312233           sd
## 2 rs55872725 -0.09583174 0.00312233           sd
## 3 rs11642015 -0.09581344 0.00312233           sd
head(original[, c("rsid", "beta", "se", "effect_scale")], 3)
##         rsid       beta         se effect_scale
## 1  rs1421085  0.4667140 0.01520618     original
## 2 rs55872725 -0.4667140 0.01520618     original
## 3 rs11642015 -0.4666249 0.01520618     original

Here original_sd is 4.87 kg/m², estimated from the source’s own effect sizes and allele frequencies (original_sd_method == "estimated_from_source_maf"). Log-odds effects are returned unchanged, since log odds are their original units. When an Analysis stored per SD isn’t a continuous trait with a recorded phenotype SD, opengwasr refuses rather than guess. That includes the binary Analyses stored per SD (the 1,846 binary ukb-b-* traits), which have no phenotype SD to rescale by:

og_tophits(src, "OGS-00009:ukb-b-19953", clump = FALSE, original_units = TRUE)
## Error in `og_tophits()`:
## ! Can't give this Analysis in original units.
## ✖ `OGS-00009:ukb-b-19953`: it has no recorded phenotype SD (`original_sd`).
## ℹ Use `original_units = FALSE` (the default) for per-SD effects.

That error has class opengwasr_original_units_unavailable, a kind of opengwasr_refusal. Its ids field lists the Analyses it refused, and reason says why for each: "binary_per_sd", "no_original_sd" or "unknown_trait_type" (the trait isn’t recorded as continuous). It is raised before the query runs. Asking for several Analyses refuses them all if any can’t be rescaled.

Sample size

og_analyses() returns the API’s own metadata names (sample_size, n_cases, n_controls). Associations carry the names MR methods expect: n, ncase and ncontrol. n is the per-Association sample size where the GWAS Store holds one, and otherwise the Analysis’s sample_size. Some GWAS Stores, such as the molecular-trait one, send an n on each Association; most don’t, and then every Association has the Analysis’s sample_size. sample_size_kind, ncase and ncontrol always describe the Analysis’s own count, not where a row’s n came from. sample_size_kind says what kind of count that is, so an effective N is never mistaken for a count of participants:

  • "total": participants in the Analysis.
  • "case_control": cases plus controls. ncase and ncontrol give each.
  • "variant_level": N differs from variant to variant, as in many molecular-trait Analyses.
out <- og_tophits(src, c("OGS-00011:GCST003116", "OGS-00027:ENSG00000000419"),
                  clump = FALSE, limit = 5)
out[c(1, 6:8), c("id", "n", "sample_size_kind", "ncase", "ncontrol", "effect_scale")]
##                          id      n sample_size_kind ncase ncontrol effect_scale
## 1      OGS-00011:GCST003116 187599     case_control 61289   126310       log_or
## 6 OGS-00027:ENSG00000000419  30895    variant_level    NA       NA           sd
## 7 OGS-00027:ENSG00000000419  30694    variant_level    NA       NA           sd
## 8 OGS-00027:ENSG00000000419  30508    variant_level    NA       NA           sd

For the case-control Analysis every row has the Analysis’s n. For the molecular one, n varies from variant to variant, and sample_size_kind says "variant_level".

Imputed Associations

A Reference-Completed Store Release holds, beside the Associations its source reported (Observed), an Imputed Association for most variants the source didn’t report. opengwasr includes them by default, and labels each Association in association_status. Here are BMI’s 1,000 strongest top hits looked up in CAD:

bmi_top <- og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90029007", clump = FALSE)
## Warning in og_tophits(src, "OGS-00011:GCST90029007", clump = FALSE): OGS-00011:GCST90029007 has more than 1,000 top hits at p <= 5e-08; only the strongest 1,000 were returned.
## ℹ Raise `limit` (at most 10,000) for more.
outcome <- og_associations(src, bmi_top$alid, "OGS-00011:GCST003116")
table(outcome$association_status)
## 
##  imputed observed 
##       61      938
observed <- og_associations(src, bmi_top$alid, "OGS-00011:GCST003116",
                            observed_only = TRUE)
nrow(observed)
## [1] 938

Including the Imputed Associations finds 999 of the 1,000 variants in the outcome. With only the Observed ones, 938. Report how many of the Associations you used were Imputed.

Provenance

Every Association carries the store_id and release_id it came from, and clumped data frames carry their clumping in columns too (see clumping provenance). These columns are the provenance that travels with each Association.

og_provenance(x) gives the details of the call that produced x, which no single Association can hold:

  • For a data frame from a query function: the call and its arguments, the Store Releases that answered, the Job ids, and the API’s counts, including whether limit cut anything off (total, truncated). For clumped top hits it adds how many top hits were considered, how many the LD Store didn’t hold (absent), and how many index variants resulted.
  • For an LD matrix from og_ld_matrix(): the LD used, the Job ids, and the variants the LD Store didn’t hold (absent).

It returns a list, and prints as below. It is attached to the data frame a query function returns and describes exactly those rows. After you combine data frames (rbind(), merge()) or subset rows, og_provenance() warns (class opengwasr_provenance_stale) and returns NULL when the rows no longer match, and stops with class opengwasr_no_provenance if the operation dropped the attribute altogether; keep it, or its counts, before you combine data frames.

og_provenance(top)
## ── opengwasr provenance ─────────────────
## • Query: og_tophits(threshold = 5e-08, limit = 3, observed_only = FALSE, clump = FALSE, original_units = FALSE)
## • Store Releases: OGS-00011/OGS-00011-completed
## • Jobs: 60057995
## • Rows: 3 returned of 3 matching (truncated)
## • Retrieved: 2026-11-24 14:04:41 UTC

Record the Store Releases alongside your analysis. They identify exactly which data answered.

When a query can’t be answered

opengwasr never quietly returns a different answer from the one you asked for. An option is either honoured or refused with an error saying why. Every error is a classed condition, so scripts and packages can handle particular failures.

When the API refuses a request, the error’s message is the API’s own, and its class is the API’s error code with opengwasr_ in front: the API’s unsupported_threshold is opengwasr_unsupported_threshold, and so on for every code it sends. The code itself is in e$api_error. The API’s error guide lists its codes. These are the ones you are most likely to meet:

Class When
opengwasr_unauthorized The API didn’t accept your key
opengwasr_release_not_found A Store Release you pinned isn’t served
opengwasr_unsupported_threshold, opengwasr_request_too_large, opengwasr_ld_refusal The API can’t answer exactly what you asked. These also have class opengwasr_refusal
opengwasr_user_queue_full, opengwasr_server_busy, … The API stayed busy until the call’s timeout. These also have class opengwasr_busy
opengwasr_result_expired A Job’s result had already been read, or had expired (Large queries and Jobs)
opengwasr_invalid_request, opengwasr_invalid_query The API couldn’t accept the request as sent, such as a threshold above 1
opengwasr_api_error The API answered with an error but no code

Identifiers are the exception. Every function that takes Analyses looks them up first, and the API’s lookup lists the identifiers it can’t resolve rather than refusing them. For those, opengwasr writes the message, quoting the API’s reason where it gives one, but the class and e$api_error are the API’s codes all the same, so a handler doesn’t need to know which way the error came:

Class When
opengwasr_analysis_not_found An identifier names no Analysis. A retired one also has class opengwasr_analysis_retired
opengwasr_ambiguous_analysis An identifier names more than one Analysis
opengwasr_release_not_found, opengwasr_release_selection_required A GWAS Store id in releases isn’t served, or a GWAS Store serves several Store Releases and you must pin one

Elsewhere opengwasr writes its own message only where the API can’t speak:

Class When
opengwasr_auth No key, or no API URL, is set
opengwasr_argument An argument is the wrong kind, such as ids that aren’t character
opengwasr_original_units_unavailable original_units = TRUE can’t be honoured. Also opengwasr_refusal
opengwasr_timeout, opengwasr_job_failed, opengwasr_interrupted A Job didn’t finish in time, failed (with the API’s reason as the message), or you interrupted the wait (Large queries and Jobs)
opengwasr_unreachable The API couldn’t be reached

All of them also have class opengwasr_error. Catch one by its class:

info <- tryCatch(
  og_analyses(src, c("ukb-b-19953", "ieu-a-2")),
  opengwasr_analysis_not_found = function(e) {
    message("Skipping: ", paste(e$ids, collapse = ", "))
    og_analyses(src, setdiff(c("ukb-b-19953", "ieu-a-2"), e$ids))
  }
)
## Skipping: ieu-a-2

Each condition carries the details as fields, such as e$ids here, with the API’s reason for each, where it gave one, in e$api_reasons (a retired Analysis’s successor is in e$superseded_by). A condition raised from an API error response carries the API’s error code and message as e$api_error and e$api_message, the HTTP status as e$status, the whole body as e$api_body, and every other field of the body under its own name, such as e$indexed_thresholds above.

One warning is classed too: opengwasr_legacy_successor, when a legacy identifier is answered by a later release of its analysis (see Legacy OpenGWAS identifiers). It is a warning rather than an error because opengwasr does answer, and says which Analysis answered. It doesn’t have class opengwasr_error.
